title: Classes, objects and encapsulation
description: Classes and structs, constructors and destructors, access specifiers, const member functions and static members.

content.title: Classes and objects

choices.text: On the stack; it is destroyed automatically when play() ends
On the heap; you have to delete it
It is destroyed later by the garbage collector
It lives until the whole program ends

content.explanation: A local object has automatic storage: it is created where it is declared and destroyed at the end of the block, with no new and no delete.

content.question: What is the difference between class and struct in C++?

choices.text: Only the default access: private for class, public for struct
A struct cannot have member functions
A struct is a value type and a class a reference type
A struct cannot be inherited from

content.explanation: In C++ they are almost the same thing. The value/reference difference is true in C#, not in C++. By convention, struct is used for simple groups of public data.

choices.text: open work close end
open work end close
work end
open close work end

content.explanation: logger is created at its declaration (open), the block works, and logger is destroyed at the closing brace of its block (close), before end. This precise timing is what makes destructors so useful in C++.

content.title: Encapsulation
content.body:
A class decides who can use its members with access specifiers, written as sections:
- public: everyone.
- private: only the class's own member functions (the default in a class).
- protected: the class and the classes that inherit from it.

Encapsulation keeps the data private and lets others use it only through member functions that enforce the rules.

A member function marked const, like std::string bark() const, promises not to change the object. Only const member functions can be called on a const object.

choices.text: It does not compile: balance_ is private
The balance becomes -500
deposit is called automatically with -500
It compiles, but crashes at run time

content.explanation: Access is checked by the compiler. The only way to change the balance is deposit, which rejects negative amounts: that is encapsulation.

content.question:
std::string bark() const { ... }

What does the const after the parentheses mean?

choices.text: bark promises not to change the object, and can be called on a const object
bark always returns the same string
The returned string cannot be changed
bark can only be called once

content.explanation: The compiler refuses any change to the data members inside a const member function. Marking read-only functions const is part of a good class design.

choices.text: It does not compile

content.explanation: A static data member belongs to the class, not to each object: the three constructors increment the same counter.

content.question: Which are good encapsulation habits in C++?

choices.text: Keep the data members private
Mark the member functions that do not change the object const
Make every member public, it is simpler
Return a non-const reference to private data so callers can change it freely

content.explanation: Returning a non-const reference to a private member lets anyone change it and bypass the class's rules: it breaks encapsulation as much as making it public.
